newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela police to treat pilots better - union.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela police to treat pilots better - union.

text.p: Venezuelan ship pilots withdrew a strike threat which could have hit the country's main oil export route after talks with police on Monday, a union leader said.

The pilots' union had threatened to paralyse traffic through the Lake Maracaibo shipping lane because of complaints about police brutality and the lack of maintenance in the channel which has seen three oil tankers seriously grounded so far this year.

The union had all but withdrawn its threat last week after the Lake Maracaibo port captain introduced a 36-foot draught restriction, down from a normal 39.5 foot. On Monday, police assurances of better treatment erased any possibility of action.
"The issues which lead to this conflict have been solved... We no longer have any reason to strike," said pilot union spokesman Fidel Sanchez.

"The commander in chief of the Guardia Nacional gave instructions to the regional commander and they are aware that in these cases they have to act according to the rules and not in an arbitrary fashion," Sanchez said. He said a radio operator on one ship had been beaten after a grounding in the channel.
Venezuela's Navy is currently doing an underwater survey of the channel as part of an investigation into the groundings, one of which produced an oil spill of at least 25,000 barrels of oil.

Shipping sources in Maracaibo say the channel is so poorly maintained that oil tankers habitually touch bottom as they leave. It is dredged by a state-run Institution Nacional de Canalizaciones whose president was sacked by the Minister of Transport last week.

Ship brokers and other sources say the 3.5 foot draught reduction could cut Venezuela's oil exports by about 150,000 barrels per day because each 500,000-barrel tanker will be able to load about 50,000 barrels less than usual.
The channel is also an important export route for coal, gas and petrochemical products.
